paragraphs.heading: What bird flight is
paragraphs.text: Flying is the main way most birds get around. It helps them find food, breed, escape predators and migrate. Flight covers several kinds of motion, from hovering to taking off and landing, each built from many complex movements. Over millions of years, species evolved specialized wings and styles of flight to suit their own environments, prey and predators.

paragraphs.heading: Lift, drag and thrust
paragraphs.text: Birds fly on principles similar to those of aircraft, held up by three aerodynamic forces: lift, drag and thrust. Lift comes from air flowing over the wing, which is an airfoil, a shape that makes the air push the wing up while the air itself is sent downward. Drag is the force that acts against the direction of travel, so it is where flight loses energy, and a streamlined body and wings reduce it. Aircraft get thrust from engines, but birds make it by flapping their wings with a certain amplitude and frequency.

paragraphs.heading: Gliding and flapping
paragraphs.text: Birds use three main kinds of flight, told apart by how the wings move. In gliding, no power is used and the upward force equals the bird's weight. The energy lost to drag is paid for either by losing height or by riding rising air currents called thermals, which is known as soaring. In flapping flight the wings still make lift, but the flight muscles tilt it forward to give thrust. The downstroke gives most of the thrust, and on each upstroke the wing folds in a little to save energy.

paragraphs.heading: Bounding and hovering
paragraphs.text: Small birds often cover long distances by bounding flight, in which short bursts of flapping alternate with spells when the wings are folded against the body and the bird follows a mostly ballistic path. This is thought to save energy by cutting drag during the folded phase. True hovering means making lift by flapping alone rather than by moving through the air, and its high energy cost usually limits it to smaller birds. Hummingbirds are the family specialized for it: their wings stay extended through a figure-of-eight stroke that makes lift on both the upstroke and the downstroke, beating some 43 times a second, and in others as many as 80.

paragraphs.heading: Taking off and landing
paragraphs.text: Taking off is one of the most energy-hungry parts of flight, because the bird must get enough air moving over its wings to make lift. Small birds simply jump upward. Larger birds such as albatrosses and swans need a running start, and large birds also face into the wind or drop off a branch or cliff. Landing is hard for large birds with high wing loads too; some aim below the target, such as a cliff nest, then pull up so they arrive with almost no airspeed. Some large birds such as geese lose height fast by sideslipping from side to side or even turning briefly upside down, a move called whiffling.

paragraphs.heading: Wings and their origins
paragraphs.text: The wings, which are a bird's forelimbs, are the key to flight. Each has a central vane built from three limb bones: the humerus, ulna and radius. Several theories try to explain how bird flight first evolved. They include falling or gliding down from trees, running or leaping up from the ground, running up slopes with help from the wings, and pouncing.
